working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Walking Golfers
angle: A practical, opinionated decision guide framed around the realities of UK courses (hilly parklands, exposed links, wet fairways, small car boots) rather than a generic product roundup. The post helps a regular walking golfer work out which type genuinely suits their game and circumstances, without assuming either option is automatically better.
research_notes:
- Push trolleys are significantly cheaper than electric equivalents and never need charging between rounds; key practical advantage for golfers who sometimes forget or can't charge overnight
- Electric trolleys are heavier due to motor and battery, but the weight is largely irrelevant once on the course since you are not pushing the load yourself; weight matters mainly when lifting in/out of the boot
- Push trolleys typically offer more built-in storage as standard (phone, balls, tees, umbrella slot); electric models often require paid accessory add-ons for the same functionality
- Three-wheel push trolleys track straighter and are more stable on uneven ground than two-wheel pull trolleys; pushing is easier on the body than pulling/twisting
- Electric models have advanced braking and better traction on slopes; meaningfully better on hilly UK parkland courses
- Battery type matters: lithium batteries are lighter, faster-charging, and more reliable than older lead-acid models; 18-hole, 27-hole, and 36-hole battery capacities available — match to your typical round length and course hilliness
- Key UK brands in electric: PowaKaddy (FX and CT ranges), Motocaddy (S1, M1, M5 GPS, M7 GPS Remote), Stewart Golf Q Follow (premium follow/remote), Hill Billy Terrain (UK-built budget option)
- Key push trolley models mentioned in UK press: PowaKaddy Micra (approx. £189, 5.5 kg, ultra-lightweight), Motocaddy Cube Push (compact cube fold), Stewart R1-S (UK-made, remote-controlled steering on a push frame), Big Max Autofold FF, Clicgear 4.0
- Compact fold is important for electric trolleys specifically because the battery makes them heavier to manhandle — ease of fold matters more than for push
- Follow/remote electric trolleys (e.g. Stewart Q Follow at approx. £1,600–£1,900, Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote) are the top-end category; genuinely caddy-like experience but significant outlay
- Budget entry point for electric with lithium battery is roughly £300–£450; mid-range GPS electric roughly £450–£650; premium GPS/remote models £850–£1,900+
- For flat or gently undulating courses and budget-conscious golfers, a push trolley remains a sensible, practical choice
- Prices sourced from UK retail references in search results — treat as approximate/indicative, not guaranteed current RRP
